title: Taxi
author: Don Vaughan Don Vaughan is a freelance writer based; North Carolina
date: 2015-10-01
---
Taxi

- Awards And Honors:

- Emmy Award

- Golden Globe Award

Taxi, American television situation comedy that aired on the networks ABC for four seasons (1978–82) and NBC for one season (1983). An immediate hit with critics and viewers, Taxi is an ensemble show about taxicab drivers who work for the fictional New York City–based Sunshine Cab Company. The show helped launch the careers of actors Danny DeVito, Christopher Lloyd, and Tony Danza, and it also introduced actor and comedian Andy Kaufman to a national audience.

Taxi was created by television producers James L. Brooks, Stan Daniels, David Davis, and Ed. Weinberger. It was inspired by author Mark Jacobson's New York magazine article "Night-Shifting for the Hip Fleet" (1975), which profiled taxicab drivers working the night shift at a Greenwich Village taxi garage. The show's main protagonist, Alex Reiger (portrayed by Judd Hirsch), considers cab driving to be his profession, whereas the other drivers view it as a temporary job and a way to earn money as they pursue their dreams.

Cast and characters

The show features an eclectic crew of drivers: old hand Alex Reiger, aspiring actor Bobby Wheeler (Jeff Conaway), single mother Elaine Nardo (Marilu Henner), boxer Tony Banta (Tony Danza), and addled ex-hippie "Reverend Jim" Ignatowski (Christopher Lloyd). Overseeing the drivers is cantankerous dispatcher Louie DePalma (Danny DeVito), while mild-mannered mechanic Latka Gravas (Andy Kaufman) keeps the cabs running.

Hirsch was at the top of the producers' list to play Reiger, but he was initially hesitant, concerned that the commitment would prevent him from appearing in films and stage productions. He instructed his agent to make outrageous demands that he felt the producers would decline, but to his surprise they agreed. Taxi's opening credits also displayed Hirsch's name before the title of the show, which initially worried him, as he was fearful it would make his fellow cast members resentful.

The casting of Andy Kaufman caused difficulties over the course of the series. A stand-up comedian known for his unconventional, often radical, skits and stunts, Kaufman had little interest in appearing in a"

Taxis on TV

| As with film, New York City has been the setting for many television shows involving taxicabs. The most famous of these was the situation comedy Taxi, which originally aired from 1978 to 1982 on ABC, and from 1982 to 1983 on NBC. Aside from launching the careers of actors Judd Hirsch, Danny DeVito, Tony Danza, Christopher Lloyd, Marilu Henner and Jeff Conaway, it included controversial up-and-coming comedy star Andy Kaufman. The series won 18 Emmy Awards, and focused on the everyday lives of a handful of New York City taxi drivers and their charismatically abusive dispatcher. Other familiar shows included Hack, which starred character actor David Morse (also known for The Green Mile and a popular run of episodes on the hit Fox drama House). In a plotline on the situation comedy Friends, the character Phoebe spent some time behind the wheel of a Checker cab when her aunt bequeathed her one in her will. |"

    "snippet": "---
title: When Taxis Talked
author: New York City Taxi; Limousine Commission
date: 2017-11-13
---
When Taxis Talked

Step into my time machine and travel back with me to 1997, the year we were thinking about the OJ Simpson civil verdict, Evander Holyfield's missing ear chunk, why Mike Tyson thought it looked appetizing, and what we should all tell the Spice Girls we really, really want. It was also in 1997 that a number of prominent physicians interviewed for articles about the dangers of short stops and facial trauma in New York City taxicabs coined the term "Cab Face." In a common thread among these stories, people would say "I always felt more confident and safe in the backseat of a taxi….but then this happened….."

While this is no longer the case, New York State law had, for many decades, specifically exempted the drivers of taxicabs and other public conveyances from having to buckle up as private vehicle drivers and front seat passengers must. Nevertheless, the Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) had a problem. The bullet-resistant, acrylic partitions that had led to the term "cab face" had been a mainstay of the New York City taxicab for many years to protect drivers who, in many instances, were considered rolling ATMs by criminals in the days before credit cards became de rigueur. So many had already been voluntarily-installed that it hardly registered on the world at large that they were mandated in 1994. So what to do?

Taking a page from former TLC Commissioner Chris Lynn, who in April 1996 championed digital audio messages for passengers to remind them to take their belongings and get a receipt, the TLC decided to add an element to the program by including a buckle-up message. The first hurdle we faced in getting the project off the ground was the fact that the woman who voiced many of those messages — Ms. Victoria Drakoulis, an employee of a taximeter manufacturer — was coming under some undeserved fire for her frankly awesome Noo Yawk accent.

This being New York City, the debate raged on, but ultimately, despite popular appearances on shows like Good Morning America and the Rosie O'Donnell Show, the clock on Ms. Drakoulis' newfound fame was ticking down.

Celebrities were the way to go, we decided. "Let's get a bunch of NYC-centric celebrities to do the messages," we said"
  },

    "docid": "3676",
    "score": 16.728361906542062,
    "snippet": "---
title: Taxicab Confessions With Dakota Johnson and Sean Penn in 'Daddio'
author: Lindsey Bahr; Associated Press
date: 2024-06-26
---
It's late at night when Dakota Johnson hops into a yellow taxicab at Kennedy airport in the new film Daddio. She's just going home to Manhattan, 44th Street, between 9th and 10th avenues. And her cab driver (Sean Penn) decides to strike up a conversation that will last the duration of this nearly 100-minute ride. There is no "quiet" setting cab.

This is not a horror movie, though for some a chatty driver on an unexpectedly long trip might be close. It's not the beginning of a wild Collateral-style night either. No, these two people from different generations, different life experiences and different classes just talk about everything — life, mistakes, technology, human nature, what makes a New Yorker, absentee fathers, affairs, human nature and love."
  },

Video Guide Description: Automobiles have been hugely popular topics for the motion picture industry since camera first met motor car. This Video Guide is a list of feature films, major documentaries, and television programs with basic descriptions of each. Links will take you to each Film's Topic Page when additional info exists in the Library. We can't post all of the videos in the Library due to copyright, but when full films are available the Film's Topic Page link will be accompanied by a film projector icon. Page Sections: Staff Picks · Factual · Fictional · Bibliography · Article Index |

"Staff Picks"

Sure, there's only one person working here, but these recommendations from Library Owner Bill Crittenden are included for entertainment value or importance to film history.

| Grand Prix Starring: James Garner · Eva Marie Saint · Yves Montand Description: A fictionalized account of the 1966 Formula 1 season with a mix of fictional characters and real drivers. Toshiro Mifune has a supporting role as a race team owner, inspired by Soichiro Honda. The film includes real-life racing footage and cameo appearances by drivers including Phil Hill, Graham Hill, Juan Manuel Fangio, Jim Clark, Jochen Rindt and Jack Brabham. Other drivers who appeared in the film include Dan Gurney, Richie Ginther, Joakim Bonnier and Bruce McLaren. Bill's Note: A landmark film in motor racing cinema for its use of on-car cameras. More than just loud cars driving fast, each race sequence is filmed in a different style showcasing multiple cinema art styles of the 1960s. |

1966 Feature Film Runtime: 176 minutes Subject: Open Wheel Racing External Links: Wikipedia · IMDb |

| Gone in 60 Seconds Starring: H.B. "Toby" Halicki · Marion Busia · Jerry Daugirda Description: A historic automotive film starring, written, and produced by H.B. Halicki, who acts in the film is Maindrian Pace, a professional car thief. His ring of thieves have to steal 48 cars in 5 days, but Pace is chased across six counties in the Los Angeles area when he tries to steal a yellow 1973 Ford Mustang Mach I, code named "Eleanor." The chase scene is 34 minutes long and destroys 93 vehicles. Many of the scenes were shot without a script or even the public's knowledge that"

function.name: search
function.description: Search the full authorized BrowseComp-Plus corpus. Returns top-5 document snippets. Use discriminative terms, names and quoted concepts; refine searches as needed.

function.name: get_document
function.description: Read the document for a docid returned by search (up to 6000 tokens).
